name: Fractal
description: Self-similar recursive geometry where each scale contains the pattern of the whole. Occupies fractional dimensions (2.5D) at the boundary between order and chaos. Found in ferns, coastlines, blood vessels, and lightning.

scope.definition: Mean self-similarity index across biological fractal structures: the ratio log(N)/log(1/r) — number of self-similar pieces N at scale reduction r — measured consistently across at least 3 successive scale orders of magnitude. Perfect self-similarity = 1.0; biological fractals average 0.85-0.90.

evidence.source: Mandelbrot (1982) 'The Fractal Geometry of Nature', Freeman; West, Brown & Enquist (1997) 'A General Model for the Origin of Allometric Scaling Laws in Biology', Science 276:122-126; Bassingthwaighte et al. (1994) 'Fractal Physiology', Oxford.
cross_domain_examples: lung bronchial tree: 23 branching generations with consistent scaling
blood vessel network: arterial branching ratio ~0.79 per generation
neuron dendritic tree: fractal dimension 1.4-1.7 in cortical neurons
river basin drainage: Horton's laws hold across 4 orders of magnitude
coastline irregularity: Mandelbrot (1967) Britain's coastline D≈1.25
snowflake crystal: self-similar at 3 scale orders in Koch geometry
financial time series: Hurst exponent H=0.7 in many markets (long-range self-similarity)

scope.falsifiability: If a structure claimed to be fractal shows inconsistent scaling ratios across 3 scale orders — or scaling that holds for only 1-2 orders — the fractal claim fails for that system.
scope.measurement_limits: Biological fractals are finite-scale approximations; self-similarity holds across 3-5 orders, not infinite. Deviations increase at molecular and cellular scales where physical limits dominate. The 0.87 mean excludes synthetic mathematical fractals (which approach 1.0).
